youtube.baslik: How the Auditory Nerve Codes Frequency and Intensity | Lesson 49 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Auditory nerve fibers code the frequency of a sound by which fiber fires (place coding) and by the timing of spikes (phase locking), and its intensity by firing rate and the number of active fibers. In this lesson we look at tuning curves, the rate-level function, the three fiber groups by spontaneous rate, and what these principles mean in the clinic.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Gelfand, Hearing: An Introduction to Psychological and Physiological Acoustics; Pickles, An Introduction to the Physiology of Hearing; Moore, An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing; Liberman (1978), Auditory-nerve response from cats raised in a low-noise chamber, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America; Kujawa and Liberman (2009), Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after temporary noise-induced hearing loss, Journal of Neuroscience.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: The neural code for frequency and intensity
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how auditory nerve fibers send the frequency and intensity of a sound to the brain.
We will look in turn at place coding, phase locking, firing rate and the different fiber groups.
The signal produced by the hair cells in the cochlea is carried to the brainstem by auditory nerve fibers.
In humans, the auditory nerve contains about thirty thousand afferent fibers.
About ninety to ninety five percent of these are type one fibers, which connect to the inner hair cells.
Each type one fiber receives input from only one inner hair cell, while each inner hair cell connects to several fibers.
The remaining thin type two fibers connect to many outer hair cells; their role is not yet fully understood.
So the detailed information about sound is carried mostly by the type one fibers linked to the inner hair cells.

yan.metin: Spike *count*, spike timing and where the fiber lies

cumleler: Nerve fibers carry information as short electrical pulses called action potentials.
Each spike follows the all-or-none principle; the size of a spike does not change with the intensity of the sound.
So information is stored first in the number of spikes per unit time, that is, the firing rate.
The second source is spike timing: whether spikes fall at particular moments of the sound wave.
The third source is which fibers fire, because each fiber comes from a particular place in the cochlea.
Now let us see how these three sources represent frequency and intensity.
The first way to code frequency is place coding.
For each frequency, the traveling wave reaches its largest amplitude at a particular place on the basilar membrane.
High-frequency sounds create the strongest vibration at the base of the cochlea, low-frequency sounds at the apex.
Fibers linked to the inner hair cells in that region fire the most, so which fiber is active signals the frequency.
This frequency map is called tonotopy, and it is preserved from the cochlear nucleus up to the cortex.
In this example, a four thousand hertz sound creates the largest vibration near the base of the cochlea.

maddeler.metin: With damage the tip is lost, curve _broadens_

cumleler: A fiber does not respond to every frequency with the same sensitivity.
The frequency at which a fiber responds at the lowest intensity is called its characteristic frequency.
If we plot its thresholds at different frequencies, we get a tuning curve shaped like the letter V.
The sharp tip of the curve comes from the outer hair cells, which work as the cochlear amplifier.
When the outer hair cells are damaged, the tip is lost; the fiber's threshold rises and its tuning curve broadens.
This partly explains why people with sensorineural loss struggle to separate sounds and to understand in noise.

notlar.metin: Intervals are multiples of the period

cumleler: The second way to code frequency is timing.
In each period, a low-frequency sound wave reaches the phase that stimulates the hair cell most, once.
Auditory nerve fibers tend to fire at exactly this phase; this is called phase locking.
A fiber does not have to fire in every period, but when it does fire, it does so at the same phase of the wave.
So the intervals between spikes are multiples of the period, and the brain can extract frequency from this pattern.
In this example, the period of a two hundred fifty hertz tone is four milliseconds.

sahneler.baslik: The volley principle and the *upper limit*

maddeler.metin: One fiber: _a few hundred_ spikes a second

cumleler: A single fiber can fire at most a few hundred spikes a second, which alone is not enough to follow a one thousand hertz wave.

cumleler.yazi: According to Wever's volley principle, different fibers fire in different periods and as a group mark every period.

cumleler: In this way the fiber population can carry the timing of the wave even at frequencies a single fiber cannot follow.
However, phase locking gradually weakens above about one thousand hertz.
In mammals, no clear phase locking is seen above about four to five kilohertz.
The exact upper limit in humans is debated, but it is accepted that timing information decreases at high frequencies.

ogeler.metin: Works across the whole frequency range
Information mostly from the place code

cumleler: Place coding gives information across the whole frequency range.
Because phase locking is lost, frequency information at high frequencies relies largely on place coding.
The sharpness of the place code depends on healthy outer hair cells.
At low and mid frequencies, place and timing information are used together.
The finer pitch discrimination at these frequencies is partly attributed to timing information.
Cochlear implants convey frequency mainly by electrode position, that is, by the place code; fine timing information remains limited.

maddeler.metin: The ear: about a _120 dB_ range

cumleler: The basic way to code intensity is firing rate: as the sound gets louder, the fiber fires more spikes per second.
The curve showing how firing rate changes with sound level is called the rate-level function.
The curve starts to rise at threshold, increases over a certain range and then saturates; the rate stops rising even if the sound does.
The dynamic range of a single fiber is usually only about twenty to forty decibels.
Yet the human ear can handle an intensity range of about one hundred twenty decibels.
To see how this gap is closed, we need to look at the spontaneous rate of the fibers.
Fibers fire on their own even without sound; this rate is called the spontaneous rate.
In Liberman's classic study in cats, fibers were divided into three groups by their spontaneous rate.
High spontaneous rate fibers, firing more than eighteen spikes a second, make up about sixty percent of fibers.
These fibers respond to very low intensities but saturate quickly after a narrow range.
Medium spontaneous rate fibers make up about a quarter, and low spontaneous rate fibers about fifteen percent.
Low spontaneous rate fibers have higher thresholds, but keep working at high intensities without saturating.
The proportions vary by species and study, but the principle is the same: different fibers cover different intensity ranges.

maddeler.metin: Fibers with different thresholds join _in turn_
The brain _combines_ rate and fiber count

cumleler: The wide intensity range is covered by fibers with different thresholds joining in turn.
Also, as the sound gets louder, basilar membrane vibration spreads from the characteristic place to neighbouring regions.
Because of this spread, fibers over a wider region, and so more fibers in total, fire.
The brain perceives intensity by weighing the firing rates together with how many fibers are active.
At high intensities, this spread also reduces frequency selectivity somewhat.
When a sound begins, fibers fire at a very high rate for the first few milliseconds.
As the sound continues, the firing rate falls and settles at a lower level; this is called adaptation.
Adaptation emphasises the onset of a sound and helps changing sounds to be noticed more easily.
When a brief stimulus makes many fibers fire at once, it creates the first wave of the auditory brainstem response, or ABR.
That is why wave one of the ABR reflects the synchronous activity of the auditory nerve.
In this example, the air-conduction thresholds of both ears are within normal limits.
But the person says they struggle to understand speech in crowded, noisy places.
Animal studies showed that noise can reduce the synapses between hair cells and nerve fibers without permanently changing thresholds.
This is called cochlear synaptopathy, a loss of the connections between hair cells and nerve fibers.
The loss is thought to hit mainly low spontaneous rate fibers; the fibers that set threshold are spared, so the audiogram can stay normal.
In humans, how common this is and how to measure it are still debated; this example only illustrates the concept.

ogeler.metin: Outer hair cells: tuning curve broadens

cumleler: These coding principles help us understand many complaints we see in the clinic.
With outer hair cell loss, tuning curves broaden and sounds become harder to separate.

cumleler.yazi: The same loss also reduces cochlear compression; loudness grows abnormally fast above threshold, which is called recruitment.

cumleler: With ageing, the timing precision of nerve fibers has been reported to decline, which can make understanding in noise harder.
In cochlear implant users, frequency information is conveyed mainly by electrode position, that is, by the place code.
In cochlear synaptopathy, difficulty understanding in noise can come to the fore while thresholds stay normal.

sahneler.metin: A normal audiogram does not rule out a complaint of understanding in noise. Take the complaint seriously, extend the assessment with speech-in-noise tests and report the results together.
cumleler: A clinical tip: a normal audiogram does not guarantee that every part of the hearing system is healthy.
The audiogram mainly measures threshold, that is, the response of the most sensitive fibers.
For someone who complains of understanding in noise, extend the assessment with additional tests such as speech-in-noise tests.
Stating the complaint and the test results together in the report gives a valuable record for later assessments.
Frequency is represented by which fibers fire, that is, by place coding.
At low and mid frequencies, phase locking adds timing information; above about four to five kilohertz this information is lost.
Intensity is coded by the increase in firing rate and by the number of active fibers.
High, medium and low spontaneous rate fibers together cover a wide intensity range.

sahneler.soru: Above roughly which frequency is phase locking lost?
sahneler.aciklama: Phase locking weakens above 1000 Hz; at _high frequencies_ frequency information relies on the place code.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: above roughly which frequency is phase locking lost?
The correct answer is C: about four to five kilohertz.

cumleler: Phase locking starts to weaken above one thousand hertz; at higher frequencies, frequency information relies on the place code.
